summary.text: Taking \(p=3\) and \(r=2\), one finds \(a(9)-a(3)=2{,}343{,}591{,}352{,}008=3^9\cdot119{,}066{,}776\), where the cofactor is not divisible by \(3\). Hence the difference is not divisible by the formally required modulus \(3^{12}\) (though it is divisible by \(3^9\)).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
C(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=5A(n)+14C(n-1),\qquad n\geq 1.
\]

There is an important discrepancy between the canonical OEIS conjecture quoted in the question and the proposition that is actually disproved in the accepted file. The proposition in the accepted file uses the modulus
\[
p^3\,p^r\,p^{2r}\,p^3=p^{3r+6},
\]
not the OEIS modulus \(p^{3r+3}\). The following gives a complete disproof of that stronger, formally stated proposition. Afterward, we check what the same calculation says about the canonical OEIS conjecture.

Consider the allowed values
\[
p=3,\qquad r=2.
\]
The number \(3\) is prime, \(3\geq 3\), and \(2\geq 2\), so this pair satisfies every hypothesis in the universal assertion. The two sequence indices are
\[
p^r=3^2=9,
\qquad
p^{r-1}=3^{2-1}=3.
\]
For the modulus occurring in the accepted formal statement, this specialization gives
\[
p^3p^rp^{2r}p^3
 =3^3\cdot3^2\cdot3^4\cdot3^3
 =3^{3+2+4+3}
 =3^{12}
 =531{,}441.
\]
It therefore suffices to show that \(a(9)-a(3)\) is not divisible by \(3^{12}\).

We first evaluate \(a(3)\). For \(A(3)\), the four summands
\(
\binom 3k^2\binom{3+k}{k}^2
\)
for \(k=0,1,2,3\) are respectively
\[
1,\quad 144,\quad 900,\quad 400.
\]
For example, these are obtained directly as
\[
\begin{aligned}
k=0 &: \binom30^2\binom30^2=1,\\
k=1 &: \binom31^2\binom41^2=3^2\cdot4^2=144,\\
k=2 &: \binom32^2\binom52^2=3^2\cdot10^2=900,\\
k=3 &: \binom33^2\binom63^2=1^2\cdot20^2=400.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
A(3)=1+144+900+400=1445.
\]
Because the second term in \(a(3)\) is \(C(3-1)=C(2)\), we also calculate the three summands
\(
\binom2k^2\binom{2+k}{k}
\)
for \(k=0,1,2\). They are
\[
1,\quad 12,\quad 6,
\]
since
\[
\binom20^2\binom20=1,
\qquad
\binom21^2\binom31=2^2\cdot3=12,
\qquad
\binom22^2\binom42=1^2\cdot6=6.
\]
Thus
\[
C(2)=1+12+6=19,
\]
and hence
\[
a(3)=5A(3)+14C(2)
=5\cdot1445+14\cdot19
=7225+266
=7491.
\]

We next evaluate \(a(9)\). Direct substitution into the defining finite sum gives the following complete list of the summands of \(A(9)\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
k&\displaystyle \binom9k^2\binom{9+k}{k}^2\\ \hline
0&1\\
1&8{,}100\\
2&3{,}920{,}400\\
3&341{,}510{,}400\\
4&8{,}116{,}208{,}100\\
5&63{,}631{,}071{,}504\\
6&176{,}752{,}976{,}400\\
7&169{,}612{,}185{,}600\\
8&47{,}869{,}064{,}100\\
9&2{,}363{,}904{,}400
\end{array}
\]
Adding these ten integers yields
\[
A(9)=468{,}690{,}849{,}005.
\]

The other term needed is \(C(8)\). Its summands are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
k&\displaystyle \binom8k^2\binom{8+k}{k}\\ \hline
0&1\\
1&576\\
2&35{,}280\\
3&517{,}440\\
4&2{,}425{,}500\\
5&4{,}036{,}032\\
6&2{,}354{,}352\\
7&411{,}840\\
8&12{,}870
\end{array}
\]
Their sum is
\[
C(8)=9{,}793{,}891.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
 &=5A(9)+14C(8)\\
 &=5\cdot468{,}690{,}849{,}005
   +14\cdot9{,}793{,}891\\
 &=2{,}343{,}454{,}245{,}025
   +137{,}114{,}474\\
 &=2{,}343{,}591{,}359{,}499.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)-a(3)
 &=2{,}343{,}591{,}359{,}499-7{,}491\\
 &=2{,}343{,}591{,}352{,}008.
\end{aligned}
\]
This difference factors as
\[
2{,}343{,}591{,}352{,}008
 =19{,}683\cdot119{,}066{,}776
 =3^9\cdot119{,}066{,}776.
\]
The second factor is not divisible by \(3\): its decimal digit sum is
\[
1+1+9+0+6+6+7+7+6=43,
\]
and \(43\) is not divisible by \(3\). Thus the exact exponent of \(3\) dividing \(a(9)-a(3)\) is \(9\). In particular, \(3^{12}\) does not divide this difference. Equivalently,
\[
a(9)\not\equiv a(3)\pmod{3^{12}}.
\]
For an explicit remainder check, division by \(3^{12}=531{,}441\) gives
\[
a(9)-a(3)
 =531{,}441\cdot4{,}409{,}880+314{,}928,
\]
with nonzero remainder \(314{,}928\).

The pair \((p,r)=(3,2)\) therefore contradicts the assertion that, for every prime \(p\geq3\) and every \(r\geq2\),
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})
 \pmod{p^3p^rp^{2r}p^3}.
\]
This completes the disproof of the proposition actually stated in the accepted file.

However, this is not a disproof of the canonical OEIS conjecture as quoted in the question. For that conjecture the modulus at \((p,r)=(3,2)\) is
\[
p^{3r+3}=3^{3\cdot2+3}=3^9=19{,}683.
\]
The factorization above shows precisely that
\[
3^9\mid a(9)-a(3),
\]
so in fact
\[
a(9)\equiv a(3)\pmod{3^9}.
\]
Hence the accepted counterexample refutes the stronger modulus \(p^{3r+6}\), but it does not refute the canonical modulus \(p^{3r+3}\). No disproof of the canonical conjecture follows from the accepted argument.
